for_students:
Your Career Compass is a starting point, not a final answer. It shows which kinds of work tend to energise you, based on your interests right now, and interests grow and shift as you try new things. Use it to explore, not to box yourself in, whether you are 16 and choosing subjects or 46 and wondering what comes next.

Start by reading the careers listed under your top letters and marking three that make you curious. Then do some real-world research: watch a day-in-the-life video, message someone who already works in that field, or ask a friend or relative in that profession what their week actually looks like. Check entry routes early, because admission tests, licensing rules and subject requirements differ by country, and at school many start with the subjects you choose at 15 or 16.

If you are changing careers or returning to work after a break, start from the skills you already have: leading people, handling money, caring for family, staying calm under pressure. They count. A degree is one route; apprenticeships, short courses, part-time study, bootcamps, portfolios and freelancing are others, and in 2026 many employers care about what you can do as much as where or when you studied.

Finally, talk to the people your choice affects, whether that is your parents, a partner or your own children, with your results in hand. Share what excites you, listen properly to their concerns, and look for paths that honour both your interests and their hopes.
for_parents:
Your child's Career Compass is a window into what naturally interests and motivates them. It is not a verdict, and it does not replace your guidance. Used respectfully, it can turn a tense conversation about the future into a shared exploration.

Read the report together and ask open questions: 'Which of these surprised you?' 'What would a good working day look like for you?' Listen more than you speak. Many parents find their child's interests fit more fields than they expected; a child who loves helping people may thrive in medicine, but also in psychology, nursing, teaching or physiotherapy.

Many parents have made real sacrifices so their children could have security, and wanting a 'safe' career for your child is love, not control. Still, try not to push a field only because of 'what will people say', relatives' opinions or what was prestigious a generation ago. Today's job market rewards skills, adaptability and genuine interest, and a motivated person in a less famous field often outperforms an unhappy one in a 'safe' field.

Be honest about practical realities such as fees, distance from home and family responsibilities, and share your own experience of work, including the turns you didn't plan. The same applies if your child is already grown and changing direction. Above all, your support matters more than any test. Someone who feels trusted to choose, and knows their family stands behind them, has the strongest possible start.

faq.q: My family expects a particular career, but my results point elsewhere. What should I do?
faq.a: First, don't use the report as a weapon in an argument. Share it calmly and explain what excites you and why. Ask what your family hopes that career will give you: security, respect, a life of service? Then show them careers that offer the same things; someone steered towards medicine might find them in pharmacy, psychology, biomedical engineering or healthcare data. If you're genuinely unsure, spend a few weeks shadowing someone in the expected field, volunteering or trying a short course, and see how it feels. A respectful, informed conversation usually works far better than a standoff.

faq.q: My top code doesn't match what I studied or the work I do now. Is it too late?
faq.a: Not at all. Most interest areas connect with several subject combinations and many jobs. A Maths and Physics student with a strong Artistic score can move into architecture, UI/UX design or game development, while an accountant with a strong Social score might enjoy teaching, coaching or HR. Many universities and colleges accept students from different backgrounds, sometimes with a foundation year, bridging or conversion course, and employers increasingly hire career changers for their experience. Look for the overlap rather than starting from scratch.

faq.q: Can I build a career through freelancing without a university degree?
faq.a: Yes, and many people already do, from students earning their first income to parents and retirees working flexible hours, especially in design, writing, video editing, development, digital marketing and bookkeeping. Free or low-cost online courses can get you started. Build a portfolio, begin with small projects and collect good reviews. That said, a degree still helps for visas, government jobs, regulated professions and some corporate roles, so many people combine freelancing with a part-time or online degree.

faq.q: How accurate is the Career Compass?
faq.a: It reflects your interests based on your answers today, using the well-established Holland interest framework. It does not measure intelligence, ability or the grades you'll get in an exam. Your results can shift as you gain experience, so retake it after a year or after a big change like starting university or a new job. Treat it as a well-informed conversation starter, and combine it with your grades, practical considerations and advice from teachers and working professionals.

faq.q: My results show two very different letters. Which one should I follow?
faq.a: You don't have to choose. Mixed codes, like Artistic with Conventional or Realistic with Social, often point to unusual and valuable careers. An A-C person might excel in architectural documentation, UX research or publishing. An R-S person might thrive in physiotherapy, emergency services or vocational teaching. Look for roles that use both sides of you, and remember that hobbies and side projects can satisfy an interest your main job doesn't.

faq.q: Should I study abroad or stay close to home?
faq.a: Your Career Compass tells you what you might enjoy, not where to study it. Weigh the costs, scholarships (such as Chevening, Fulbright, DAAD and university awards), visa and post-study work rules, and whether your field has strong options where you already live. Professions like medicine, law and nursing have licensing rules that differ by country, so check them before you choose where to train. Many students complete a strong bachelor's close to family and move for a master's, which is often shorter, more affordable and more focused. If you have a partner, children or a job to think about, talk honestly about what a move would mean for everyone.
